questions.title: Cache-Aside Pattern with Spring
questions.question: How does the cache-aside pattern work and how do you implement it with Spring Cache and Redis?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Cache-aside (lazy loading): application checks cache first; on miss, loads from DB and populates cache
- Spring @Cacheable: transparent caching — no manual cache logic needed
- @CacheEvict: invalidate cache on update/delete to keep cache and DB consistent
- @CachePut: update cache without eviction (used for write-through pattern)
- TTL (Time-To-Live): expire cached entries — prevents serving stale data indefinitely
- Cache key: default is method parameters; customize with SpEL expressions
- Serialization: configure RedisTemplate to serialize objects as JSON (not Java serialization)
- Null caching: avoid cache stampede — cache null results to prevent repeated DB hits

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Cache-aside, also called lazy loading, is the most common caching pattern. When the application needs data, it first checks the cache. If the data is there — a cache hit — it returns immediately without touching the database. If not — a cache miss — it fetches from the database, stores the result in the cache for future requests, and returns the data. This pattern is lazy: data only enters the cache when it's actually requested.

Spring Cache makes this almost invisible. The @Cacheable annotation on a service method automatically implements the check-and-load logic. Spring checks if a result is cached for the given key; if so, returns it without executing the method; if not, executes the method and caches the result before returning. You write normal service code and the caching just works.

The critical counterpart is @CacheEvict for maintaining consistency. When you update or delete a user, the cached version is stale. Annotating the update method with @CacheEvict removes that entry from Redis, forcing the next read to fetch fresh data from the database. A common mistake is forgetting to evict on updates, which leads to users seeing outdated data until the TTL expires.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

questions.title: Cache Invalidation Strategies
questions.question: What are the different cache invalidation strategies and when do you use each?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- TTL-based expiration: simplest — stale data accepted until TTL expires
- Explicit invalidation: evict specific key on data change — consistent but complex
- Write-through: update cache on every write — always fresh, higher write latency
- Write-behind (write-back): write to cache immediately, sync to DB asynchronously — risk of data loss
- Event-driven invalidation: publish event on data change → consumers evict cache — decoupled
- Tag-based invalidation: group related keys by tag → invalidate entire group at once
- Cache invalidation is 'one of the two hard things in CS' — understand the trade-offs

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Cache invalidation is famously one of the hardest problems in computer science because stale data in a cache can cause subtle, hard-to-debug bugs. The right strategy depends on how critical freshness is and how frequently data changes.

TTL-based expiration is the simplest — you accept that cached data can be up to N minutes stale. This is fine for data that changes infrequently or where a short window of staleness doesn't matter, like a product catalog or user profile. The TTL acts as a backstop against serving permanently stale data if explicit invalidation fails.

Explicit invalidation on writes gives you stronger consistency. When a user updates their profile, you immediately evict their cached entry. The next read misses the cache and fetches fresh data. This is what Spring's @CacheEvict implements. The challenge is keeping the invalidation logic in sync with all the ways data can change — if you add a new update path and forget to evict, you introduce a stale cache bug.

For microservices, event-driven invalidation is cleaner. The service that owns the data publishes an event when data changes. Cache consumers subscribe and evict the relevant key. This decouples the publisher from knowing which consumers have cached its data, and is resilient to adding new consumers without changing the publisher.

questions.title: Redis for Session Management and Rate Limiting
questions.question: How do you use Redis for distributed session management and rate limiting in a Spring Boot application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Spring Session: store HTTP sessions in Redis — enables stateless, scalable backends behind load balancers
- Session persistence: sessions survive server restarts and work across multiple app instances
- Rate limiting: count requests per IP/user in a sliding window using Redis sorted sets or counter+TTL
- Sliding window counter: Redis sorted set with timestamp as score; ZREMRANGEBYSCORE + ZCARD for count
- Fixed window counter: INCR + EXPIRE — simpler, slight boundary burst allowed
- Lua scripts: atomic rate limit operations (INCR + EXPIRE in single atomic call)
- Redis Modules: RedisRateLimiter in Spring Cloud Gateway uses token bucket algorithm

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Spring Session with Redis solves a fundamental scalability problem. If HTTP sessions are stored in the application's memory, every request from a user must go to the same server instance — sticky sessions. If that instance fails, the session is lost. With Spring Session, sessions are stored in Redis, any server instance can handle any request, and sessions survive server restarts.

For rate limiting, Redis is the standard tool because of its atomic operations. The simplest approach is a counter per IP with a TTL — increment it on each request, set a TTL of the window duration on the first increment. If the counter exceeds the limit, reject the request. The limitation is a boundary burst: a user can exhaust their limit at the end of one window and immediately use the full limit at the start of the next.

A sliding window counter using a sorted set is more accurate. You store each request timestamp as a member with the timestamp as the score. To count requests in the last minute, you remove entries older than 60 seconds and count remaining members. This prevents the boundary burst but uses more memory. For production rate limiting at scale, Spring Cloud Gateway's RedisRateLimiter uses a token bucket algorithm, which is a good off-the-shelf solution.

speakable_v2.cap: For production rate limiting at scale, Spring Cloud Gateway's RedisRateLimiter uses a token bucket algorithm, which is a good off-the-shelf solution.

questions.title: Write-Through and Write-Behind Patterns
questions.question: What are write-through and write-behind caching patterns and when do you use them?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Write-through: write to cache AND database synchronously on every write — cache always fresh
- Write-behind (write-back): write to cache immediately, async write to DB later — lower write latency
- Write-through: higher write latency (both cache + DB in sync), no stale data
- Write-behind: risk of data loss if cache crashes before DB write; eventual consistency
- Spring @CachePut: implements write-through — updates cache with return value
- Write-behind in Spring: custom implementation needed; not provided out of the box
- Use write-through when: reads must see fresh data immediately after writes
- Use write-behind when: write throughput > what DB can handle; some data loss acceptable

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Write-through maintains cache and database in sync on every write. When an update happens, you update the database and update the cache in the same operation. Reads always hit the cache and see fresh data. The cost is slightly higher write latency — you're doing two writes instead of one — and more cache churn if many items are written but rarely read.

Write-behind trades consistency for write throughput. Updates go to the cache immediately, and a background process periodically flushes cached updates to the database. Reads are fast and writes feel fast. The risk is data loss — if the cache node crashes before the flush, those updates are gone. Write-behind requires durable cache storage and careful recovery design.

For most Spring Boot applications with a relational database, write-through via @CachePut is the right choice. The latency difference is minimal at the scale most applications operate, and the consistency guarantee is worth it. Write-behind is appropriate for time-series data, counters, or session activity logs where loss of a few seconds of data is acceptable.

speakable_v2.hook: Write-through maintains cache and database in sync on every write.
speakable_v2.cap: Write-behind is appropriate for time-series data, counters, or session activity logs where loss of a few seconds of data is acceptable.

questions.title: Distributed Locking with Redis
questions.question: How do you implement distributed locks with Redis for preventing concurrent execution across multiple app instances?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Problem: scheduled job runs on all instances simultaneously — race condition
- SET NX EX: atomic set-if-not-exists with TTL — simple distributed lock
- Must release lock: use finally block; include random token to verify ownership before delete
- TTL: prevent deadlock if lock holder crashes — must exceed job execution time
- Redlock: Redisson's algorithm — multi-node lock; more robust than single-node
- Redisson: RLock implements java.util.concurrent.locks.Lock — familiar API
- @SchedulerLock (ShedLock): distributed scheduling lock with DB or Redis backend
- Watchdog: Redisson auto-extends TTL while lock is held — prevents expiry during work

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Distributed locks solve the concurrent execution problem when your application runs as multiple instances. A common example is scheduled jobs — if you have 3 app instances and a job that runs every minute, all three instances will trigger the job simultaneously without a lock.

The simplest implementation uses Redis SET with NX and EX flags — set the key only if it doesn't exist, with an expiry time. The first instance to set the key wins and executes the job. The key must expire automatically in case the winning instance crashes before releasing the lock, which would otherwise cause a deadlock.

Redisson provides a more production-ready distributed lock implementation via RLock, which includes automatic TTL extension via a watchdog thread. The watchdog keeps extending the lock TTL as long as the lock holder is alive, preventing premature expiry of long-running operations. For scheduled jobs specifically, ShedLock is a purpose-built library that works with Redis, JDBC, or other backends.

questions.title: Cache Warming and Preloading Strategies
questions.question: How do you warm up a cache on application startup to avoid cold start performance issues?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Cold cache: on startup or Redis restart, all requests miss → hit DB → thundering herd
- Cache warming: proactively populate cache on startup before serving traffic
- @PostConstruct or ApplicationReadyEvent: run warming logic at startup
- Load hot data: top products, popular categories, application config
- Thundering herd: many simultaneous cache misses — mitigate with locking or probabilistic approach
- ECS/Kubernetes: warming in readiness probe logic — don't mark ready until cache is warm
- Gradual rollout: canary deploy warms new instances before full traffic shift

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Cache warming is loading frequently accessed data into the cache before the application starts serving traffic. Without it, the first requests after deployment or a Redis restart cause a thundering herd — all cache misses simultaneously hitting the database, potentially overwhelming it and causing timeouts during exactly the period you're trying to handle traffic.

For Spring Boot, ApplicationReadyEvent fires after the application context is fully initialized and the application is ready to serve requests. This is the right place to run cache warming — after all beans are wired up but just before the load balancer starts routing traffic.

In Kubernetes, tie cache warming to the readiness probe. The pod only becomes ready after warming completes. ECS health checks serve the same purpose — the ECS service waits for the container's health check to pass before routing traffic. If your Spring Boot actuator /health endpoint includes a custom health indicator that reports unhealthy until warming is complete, you get this behavior automatically.
